core: working definition of revenue, attributed to OpenStax's Principles of Accounting (corroborated by SEC Investor.gov and CFI): the value of the goods and services a business provides to its customers
revenue vs profit: money in from sales vs what remains after costs are subtracted (net income / net loss)

when revenue is recorded: the revenue recognition principle — in the period earned, when goods are delivered or services performed, not when cash arrives (accrual idea previewed; accrual-accounting referenced as a sibling topic)
types of revenue named: sales revenue, service revenue, interest — each with one line and an original example
revenue in the statements: the top line of the income statement, which measures performance over a period (income-statement referenced as a sibling topic)
growing revenue: three levers — more customers, higher prices, more products — derived from revenue = quantity × price
the honest framing: revenue is not wealth; it is the start of the story
supporting: revenue equals quantity sold times price (Investor.gov widget formula; CFI formulas)
sold-now-paid-later sales create accounts receivable; no additional revenue is recorded when the customer pays (accounts-receivable referenced as a sibling topic)
increases in revenue raise net income and equity through the expanded accounting equation (accounting-equation referenced as a sibling topic)
revenue is also called sales (CFI usage), and revenue is the first number executives, analysts, and investors examine
outOfScope: expense categories and cost detail (owned by the expenses topic)
income statement construction, gains/losses ordering, and analysis (owned by the income-statement topic)
accrual-accounting mechanics and adjusting entries (owned by the accrual-accounting topic)
accounting equation mechanics and journalizing (owned by the accounting-equation and journal-entries topics)
GAAP revenue recognition standard detail (ASC 606 five-step model) and tax treatment of revenue

claims.claim: Revenue is the value of the goods and services a business provides to its customers; OpenStax's Principles of Accounting (Section 2.1) states this, and the SEC's Investor.gov glossary defines revenue as the total amount of money, or gross income, generated by a company from selling its goods and services. The lesson's working definition follows OpenStax and is corroborated by Investor.gov and CFI.

Revenue equals the quantity sold multiplied by the price: Investor.gov phrases it as the price of a widget times the number of widgets sold, and CFI gives the formulas units sold × average price (product businesses) and customers × average price (service businesses).

Revenue is not profit: expenses are deducted from revenue to arrive at profit or net income (CFI); OpenStax states net income occurs when revenues exceed expenses and net loss when expenses exceed revenues.

The revenue recognition principle directs a company to recognize revenue in the period in which it is earned, and revenue is not considered earned until a product or service has been provided (OpenStax Section 3.1); CFI states revenue is recorded when the company has satisfied its performance obligation to the customer, whether or not payment has been received.

When a company delivers goods or services and allows the customer to pay later, revenue is recorded at the time of delivery and the unpaid amount is recorded as accounts receivable; when the customer eventually pays, no additional revenue is recorded — cash increases and accounts receivable decrease (CFI).

Revenue sources for businesses include the sale of goods, the sale of services, and interest (CFI lists these among common corporate revenue sources); the lesson names sales revenue, service revenue, and interest revenue as types, each with an original example.

Revenue forms the top line of the income statement: CFI states revenue (also known as sales) forms the beginning of a company's income statement and is often considered the 'Top Line,' and that revenue is one of the first numbers executives, analysts, and investors analyze; OpenStax Section 2.1 describes the income statement as measuring financial performance over a period with revenues, expenses, gains, and losses as its elements.

Growing revenue follows from the revenue formula: more customers, higher prices, or more products each raise revenue, because revenue is quantity times price (derived from the Investor.gov and CFI formulas).

Revenue is not wealth: it is the start of the story, since costs are still subtracted from it before profit exists, and a business can post large revenue and still report a loss (derived from the revenue-vs-profit relationship in CFI and OpenStax).

Increases in revenue flow through the expanded accounting equation: an increase to revenue can increase net income on the income statement and change stockholders' equity on the balance sheet (OpenStax Section 3.2); the lesson references this only, since the accounting equation is a sibling topic.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Sources phrase the revenue definition differently: OpenStax says revenue is the value of goods and services a business provides to its customers; CFI says it is the value of all sales of goods and services recognized by a company in a period; Investor.gov says it is the total amount of money, or gross income, generated from selling goods and services.
positions: OpenStax Principles of Accounting, Volume 1, Section 2.1: revenue is the value of goods and services a business provides to its customers.
CFI Revenue: revenue is the value of all sales of goods and services recognized by a company in a period.
Investor.gov glossary: revenue is the total amount of money, or gross income, generated by a company from selling its goods and services.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: All three agree on the core: revenue is value earned by a business from selling goods and services. The lesson attributes the working definition to OpenStax's Principles of Accounting and notes corroboration from Investor.gov and CFI; no single wording is reproduced verbatim.

conflictingEvidence.issue: 'Sales' is used both as a synonym for total revenue (CFI: revenue is also known as sales) and as the name of one revenue type (sales revenue).
positions: CFI Revenue: revenue (also known as sales) forms the beginning of a company's income statement.
CFI Revenue sector list: the sale of goods is one revenue source among several, alongside sales of services and interest.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson notes CFI's usage that revenue is also called sales, while naming sales revenue as one type of revenue alongside service revenue and interest; the lesson's original examples keep the two uses distinct.
